# SK1064 — Use `>>>`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A cast to the unsigned type, a right shift, and a cast back is the unsigned right shift operator.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 11.0 |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

`(int)((uint)x >> n)` is three operations spelling one, and two of the three are the casts that sign extension bugs come out of — a reader has to check that the widths match before believing the round trip is lossless, and the compiler will not check it for them. `x >>> n` is the operation, at the operand's own width, with nothing to get wrong.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var high = (int)((uint)hash >> 16);
```

Write:

```csharp
var high = hash >>> 16;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The equivalence holds only where the two types are the same width, and `>>` does not preserve width below 32 bits.** `(short)((ushort)x >> n)` looks identical and is a different program: `ushort` promotes to `int` before the shift, so the value shifted is zero-extended, while `x >>> n` on a `short` promotes the *signed* value first. For `x = -1` and `n = 4` the first gives 4095 and the second gives -1. Only `int`/`uint` and `long`/`ulong` are admitted, where `>>` is defined at the declared width; `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort` and the native integer types are refused. The operand's own static type must be the signed one, so `(int)(u >> n)` on an already-unsigned `u` is not this shape. ⚠ **A `checked` context breaks the equivalence in both casts.** `(uint)x` throws for a negative `x` and `(int)u` throws for a `u` above `int.MaxValue`, where `>>>` never throws — so the rule is silent inside `checked` and silent entirely when the compilation sets `CheckForOverflowUnderflow`. ⚠ **`>>>` binds far more loosely than a cast**, so `(int)((uint)x >> n) + 1` rewritten bare would become `x >>> (n + 1)`. Rather than inventing parentheses the author did not write, the rule declines every position where the surrounding expression could rebind and fires only where a shift may stand unparenthesised. One shape with one floor, so the gate is per-rule.
